## 8. Algorithms

Three algorithms are implicit in the proofs.

**Algorithm A (Maximal packing / local cover).** Compute a maximal packing $P$ greedily: scan the vertices, adding $v$ to $P$ whenever $\operatorname{dist}(v,p) \ge 3$ for all $p$ already chosen. Then for each $p \in P$ compute a maximal independent subset $I_p$ of the radius-$2$ neighbourhood of $p$ and output $D = \bigcup_p I_p$. Correctness: maximality of $P$ makes the radius-$2$ neighbourhoods cover $V$ (Lemma 3.1 holds for maximal, not only maximum, packings), and maximality of $I_p$ makes it dominate its neighbourhood (Lemma 4.3). For geometric inputs Theorem 4.4 bounds $|I_p| \le N$, so $|D| \le N|P| \le N\rho(G)$: the output is a dominating set within a factor $N$ of optimal, together with a certificate $P$ of a matching lower bound. Complexity: $O(|V|^2)$ distance computations for the packing (or $O(|V| + |E|)$ per BFS), plus $O(\sum_p |T_p|^2)$ for the independent sets.

**Algorithm B (Interval sweep).** Sort the vertices by right endpoint. Repeatedly take the first undominated $u$, choose $d$ maximizing $r(d)$ among vertices whose interval meets $u$'s, output $d$ into $D$ and $u$ into $P$, and delete $B(d)$. This produces $|D| = |P|$, hence *simultaneously* an optimal dominating set and an optimal packing of an interval graph, certifying optimality of each by the other. Complexity $O(|V|\log|V|)$ after sorting, given the representation.

**Algorithm C (Forest sweep).** Root each component, sort by depth, and repeatedly take the deepest undominated vertex $u$, output its parent $d$ (or $u$ itself if $u$ is a root) into $D$ and $u$ into $P$, and delete $B(d)$. As in Algorithm B this yields $|D| = |P|$, certifying $\gamma(F) = \rho(F)$ constructively in $O(|V|)$ time after a BFS.

All three follow the same schema: *bank a packing centre, spend the dominators covering its radius-$2$ neighbourhood, recurse.* The size of the dominator set spent per banked centre is precisely the constant in the resulting bound.

---

## 9. Applications

**Wireless coverage with a certificate.** In a unit disk model of transmitters, Algorithm A returns a set of at most $25\rho$ relays covering all nodes, plus a set of $\rho$ mutually non-interfering nodes. The latter is a lower-bound certificate: no covering scheme can use fewer than $\rho$ relays. Thus the algorithm is a $25$-approximation whose approximation guarantee is certified per-instance, often far better than $25$.

**Facility location on the line and on trees.** Theorems 5.7 and 6.6 say that on interval and forest structures the LP-style duality is exact: the greedy sweep gives an optimal facility placement whose optimality is witnessed by an equal-size set of pairwise independent demand clusters. This is a min–max theorem with an $O(n\log n)$ constructive proof.

**Interference-aware scheduling.** A packing is a set of nodes that may transmit simultaneously with no shared receiver at distance $\le 1$. The inequality $\gamma \le N\rho$ says the cost of coverage never exceeds $N$ times the achievable parallelism — an operational statement about the trade-off between coverage cost and interference-free throughput.

**Degree-bounded networks.** Corollary 3.3 gives $\gamma \le (\Delta+1)\rho$ for every graph, which for sparse networks (small $\Delta$) is stronger than the geometric bounds and requires no embedding.

---

## 10. Discussion and future directions

The results assemble into a coherent picture.

| class | ratio $\gamma/\rho$ |
| --- | --- |
| all finite graphs | unbounded (Theorem 7.12) |
| maximum degree $\Delta$ | $\le \Delta + 1$ (Corollary 3.3) |
| forests, trees | $= 1$ (Theorem 6.6) |
| interval graphs, unit interval graphs, paths | $= 1$ (Theorem 5.7, Corollary 5.8) |
| unit interval graphs, by the metric method alone | $\le 4$, optimal for that method (Corollary 5.3, Proposition 5.2) |
| unit disk graphs | $\ge 2$ (Corollary 6.9); $\le 25$ (Theorem 4.8) |
| unit ball graphs in $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $\le 5^n$ (Theorem 4.8) |
| classes containing all Wagner unions | $\ge 3$ (Corollary 7.7) |

Three structural observations. First, the entire geometric input to Theorem 4.8 is one finite number: the maximum size of a $1$-separated set in a ball of radius $2$. Everything else is soft. Second, in dimension one the two methods separate cleanly: the metric method saturates at $4$ (Proposition 5.2), while the greedy criterion delivers the exact answer $1$. This shows the local-cover route is intrinsically lossy on structured classes, and suggests looking for greedy dominators (or greedy covers with small $c$) rather than better local packing bounds where the class allows it. Third, the additive slack in $\gamma \le c\rho + b$ is worthless against a family whose ratio persists at every scale, which is exactly what the disjoint Wagner unions supply.

### Future directions

The following directions are stated so that each could be settled by a single precise theorem.

**Conjecture 1 — the unit disk constant can be pushed to $19$, and $19$ is optimal for this proof scheme.** A closed disk of radius $2$ in the plane contains at most $19$ points that are pairwise more than $1$ apart, and $19$ is attained — for instance by the centre, a ring of six points at radius $1.05$ (mutual distance $1.05$, distance $1.05$ to the centre), and a ring of twelve points at radius $2$ offset by $15°$ (mutual distance $4\sin(\pi/12) \approx 1.035$, distance $\approx 1.023$ to the inner ring); consequently the plane has local packing bound $19$ and $\gamma \le 19\rho$ for unit disk graphs, while no bound below $19$ follows from the maximal-independent-set-in-the-radius-$2$-ball argument. The key insight is that the whole geometric input of the engine is one finite packing number — the maximum number of $1$-separated points in a disk of radius $2$ — so improving the graph theorem is exactly a planar packing problem, and the crude volume count ($25$) is the only lossy step in the entire chain.

**Direction 2 — closing the gap to the literature.** The published bounds are $\gamma \le 5\rho$ for planar graphs and $\gamma \le (18\sqrt3/\pi)\rho \approx 9.924\rho$ for unit disk graphs, against a best known lower bound of $3$ in both cases. Reproducing the planar bound requires discharging or a structural decomposition rather than the volume count; reproducing the unit disk bound requires the hexagonal-density estimate. Both are natural next targets, and both would be materially strengthened by determining the exact optimal constants, which remain open.

**Direction 3 — a characterization of the collapse.** Which graphs have a greedy dominator? Interval graphs and forests do; $C_4$ does not. A structural characterization (perhaps in terms of forbidden induced subgraphs, or of a suitable elimination ordering) would explain in one statement all classes on which $\gamma = \rho$, and the quantitative version — which graphs have a greedy cover with constant $c$? — would interpolate towards the geometric bounds.

**Direction 4 — higher dimension and other metrics.** The bound $\gamma \le 5^n\rho$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is exponentially lossy; the true growth rate of the local packing bound of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (the maximum number of $1$-separated points in a radius-$2$ ball) is a classical sphere-packing quantity of order $c^n$ with $c$ strictly below $5$. Determining the optimal exponential rate, and the corresponding statement for $\ell_p$ metrics and for doubling metric spaces (where the local packing bound is a doubling constant), would give a general theory: *any doubling metric space yields an Erdős–Pósa duality with constant its local packing number.*

**Direction 5 — algorithmic optimality.** Algorithm A is a $25$-approximation for domination in unit disk graphs with a per-instance certificate. Is the certificate ratio $\rho$-versus-$\gamma$ tight for the algorithm — that is, are there unit disk instances on which the algorithm's output is a constant factor above $\gamma$ while $\rho$ is far below $\gamma$? Understanding the worst case of the *algorithm* (rather than of the ratio) would clarify whether local covering is a good approximation strategy or only a good proof technique.

---

## 11. Conclusion

Domination and packing are dual invariants whose gap measures how badly local covering can fail to be certified locally. Without hypotheses the gap is unbounded; with bounded degree it is at most $\Delta+1$; with a one-dimensional or acyclic structure it vanishes entirely; and with a Euclidean embedding it is bounded by a purely geometric constant — the maximum number of $1$-separated points in a ball of twice the adjacency radius. The lower bound side is equally structural: the ratio $3$ realized by the Wagner graph survives disjoint unions and therefore persists at every scale, so no Erdős–Pósa inequality with a constant below $3$ is available even with additive slack. What separates the classes is precisely the presence of a *greedy dominator*: a local rule that lets one vertex pay for the whole radius-$2$ neighbourhood of the next packing centre. Where such a rule exists, covering is exactly as expensive as packing is profitable.
demo:
"""
Numerical demonstrations for the domination-packing ratio.

For a finite simple graph G on vertex set V, the radius-1 ball at v is
    B(v) = {v} union {u : u ~ v},
gamma(G) is the least size of a set meeting every B(v) via domination
(a transversal of the ball hypergraph), and rho(G) is the largest number
of pairwise disjoint balls (a matching of the same hypergraph).

This script verifies, by exhaustive computation on small instances:

  1. rho(G) <= gamma(G) for every graph (trivial duality).
  2. gamma <= (Delta + 1) * rho for every graph (degree bound).
  3. The Wagner graph V8 has rho = 1, gamma = 3, and k disjoint copies
     have rho = k, gamma = 3k, so the ratio 3 persists at every scale.
  4. The 4-cycle is a unit disk graph with gamma = 2, rho = 1.
  5. gamma = rho for paths, interval graphs and forests, with the
     earliest-endpoint and deepest-vertex greedy sweeps producing a
     dominating set and a packing of equal size.
  6. Spread graphs have rho = 1 and gamma >= k - t + 1, so the ratio is
     unbounded over all finite graphs.
  7. The local packing bound of the plane: how many points, pairwise more
     than 1 apart, fit in a disk of radius 2 (the volume count gives 25).

Everything is self-contained: only the Python standard library is used.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Vertex = int
Graph = Dict[Vertex, Set[Vertex]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic graph utilities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def make_graph(n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Build an undirected simple graph on {0, ..., n-1} from an edge list."""
    g: Graph = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        if u == v:
            raise ValueError("loops are not allowed")
        g[u].add(v)
        g[v].add(u)
    return g


def ball(g: Graph, v: Vertex) -> FrozenSet[Vertex]:
    """The radius-1 ball (closed neighbourhood) of v."""
    return frozenset({v} | g[v])


def is_dominating(g: Graph, d: Iterable[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """Does d meet the ball of every vertex?"""
    covered: Set[Vertex] = set()
    for x in d:
        covered |= ball(g, x)
    return covered == set(g)


def is_packing(g: Graph, p: Sequence[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """Are the balls of the vertices of p pairwise disjoint?"""
    for a, b in combinations(p, 2):
        if ball(g, a) & ball(g, b):
            return False
    return True


def domination_number(g: Graph) -> int:
    """gamma(G), by exhaustive search over subsets in increasing size."""
    vertices = list(g)
    for size in range(len(vertices) + 1):
        for cand in combinations(vertices, size):
            if is_dominating(g, cand):
                return size
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable: the whole vertex set dominates")


def packing_number(g: Graph) -> int:
    """rho(G), by exhaustive search over subsets in decreasing size."""
    vertices = list(g)
    for size in range(len(vertices), -1, -1):
        for cand in combinations(vertices, size):
            if is_packing(g, cand):
                return size
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable: the empty set is a packing")


def max_degree(g: Graph) -> int:
    return max((len(nbrs) for nbrs in g.values()), default=0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1-2. Trivial duality and the degree bound, on random graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def random_graph(n: int, p: float, rng: random.Random) -> Graph:
    edges = [(u, v) for u, v in combinations(range(n), 2) if rng.random() < p]
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def check_duality_and_degree_bound(trials: int = 200, n: int = 8) -> None:
    print("1-2. rho <= gamma and gamma <= (Delta+1)*rho on random graphs")
    rng = random.Random(20260820)
    worst_ratio = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        g = random_graph(n, rng.uniform(0.05, 0.6), rng)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        assert rho <= gam, (rho, gam)
        assert gam <= (max_degree(g) + 1) * rho, (gam, max_degree(g), rho)
        worst_ratio = max(worst_ratio, gam / rho)
    print(f"    {trials} random graphs on {n} vertices: both inequalities hold")
    print(f"    largest observed gamma/rho: {worst_ratio:.3f}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The Wagner graph V8 and its disjoint copies
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def wagner_graph() -> Graph:
    """V8 = Moebius ladder M4: the 8-cycle plus the four main diagonals."""
    edges = [(i, (i + 1) % 8) for i in range(8)] + [(i, i + 4) for i in range(4)]
    return make_graph(8, edges)


def disjoint_copies(g: Graph, k: int) -> Graph:
    """k disjoint copies of g, on vertices i*n + a for copy i and vertex a."""
    n = len(g)
    edges: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for i in range(k):
        for a in g:
            for b in g[a]:
                if a < b:
                    edges.append((i * n + a, i * n + b))
    return make_graph(k * n, edges)


def check_wagner() -> None:
    print("3. The Wagner graph V8 and the persistence of the ratio 3")
    w = wagner_graph()
    gam, rho = domination_number(w), packing_number(w)
    print(f"    V8: gamma = {gam}, rho = {rho}, ratio = {gam / rho:.0f}")
    assert (gam, rho) == (3, 1)
    meeting = all(ball(w, u) & ball(w, v) for u, v in combinations(range(8), 2))
    print(f"    every two closed neighbourhoods of V8 meet: {meeting}")
    for k in (1, 2, 3):
        wk = disjoint_copies(w, k)
        # gamma and rho are additive over components; verified directly for k <= 2
        rho_k = packing_number(wk) if k <= 3 else k
        gam_k = domination_number(wk) if k <= 2 else 3 * k
        print(f"    k = {k} copies: rho = {rho_k}, gamma = {gam_k}"
              f"{'' if k <= 2 else ' (gamma by additivity)'}")
        assert rho_k == k
        assert gam_k == 3 * k
    print("    no bound gamma <= c*rho + b can hold with c < 3:")
    for c, b in ((2, 5), (2, 50)):
        k = b + 1
        print(f"        c = {c}, b = {b}: at k = {k}, gamma = {3 * k} > "
              f"{c * k + b} = c*rho + b")
        assert 3 * k > c * k + b
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The 4-cycle as a unit disk graph
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def unit_disk_graph(points: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Graph:
    """Vertices are points; distinct points adjacent iff at distance <= 1."""
    n = len(points)
    edges = [
        (i, j)
        for i, j in combinations(range(n), 2)
        if math.dist(points[i], points[j]) <= 1.0
    ]
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def check_cycle4() -> None:
    print("4. The 4-cycle is a unit disk graph with gamma = 2, rho = 1")
    pts = [(0.0, 0.0), (0.8, 0.0), (0.8, 0.84), (0.0, 0.84)]
    g = unit_disk_graph(pts)
    sides = [math.dist(pts[i], pts[(i + 1) % 4]) for i in range(4)]
    diags = [math.dist(pts[0], pts[2]), math.dist(pts[1], pts[3])]
    print(f"    sides {['%.2f' % s for s in sides]} (all <= 1), "
          f"diagonals {['%.2f' % d for d in diags]} (both > 1)")
    gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
    print(f"    gamma = {gam}, rho = {rho}: the ratio already exceeds 1 in the plane")
    assert (gam, rho) == (2, 1)
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Interval graphs, paths and forests: gamma = rho by a greedy sweep
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def interval_graph(iv: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Graph:
    """Distinct vertices adjacent iff their closed intervals intersect."""
    n = len(iv)
    edges = [
        (i, j)
        for i, j in combinations(range(n), 2)
        if iv[i][0] <= iv[j][1] and iv[j][0] <= iv[i][1]
    ]
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def interval_greedy(iv: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Earliest-endpoint sweep: returns (dominating set D, packing P), |D| = |P|.

    Repeatedly take the undominated vertex u whose interval ends first, put
    into D the vertex d whose interval ends last among those meeting u, bank
    u into P, and delete everything d dominates.
    """
    g = interval_graph(iv)
    remaining: Set[int] = set(range(len(iv)))
    dom: List[int] = []
    pack: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        u = min(remaining, key=lambda x: iv[x][1])
        meeting = [x for x in range(len(iv)) if iv[x][0] <= iv[u][1] <= iv[x][1]
                   or (iv[x][0] <= iv[u][1] and iv[u][0] <= iv[x][1])]
        d = max(meeting, key=lambda x: iv[x][1])
        dom.append(d)
        pack.append(u)
        remaining -= set(ball(g, d))
    return dom, pack


def path_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return make_graph(n, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)])


def rooted_forest_greedy(g: Graph) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Deepest-vertex sweep on a forest: returns (dominating set, packing).

    Root each component, repeatedly take the deepest undominated vertex u,
    put its parent into D (or u itself if u is a root), bank u into P, and
    delete the ball of the chosen dominator.
    """
    parent: Dict[int, Optional[int]] = {}
    depth: Dict[int, int] = {}
    seen: Set[int] = set()
    for r in g:
        if r in seen:
            continue
        parent[r], depth[r] = None, 0
        seen.add(r)
        queue = [r]
        while queue:
            x = queue.pop(0)
            for y in g[x]:
                if y not in seen:
                    seen.add(y)
                    parent[y], depth[y] = x, depth[x] + 1
                    queue.append(y)
    remaining: Set[int] = set(g)
    dom: List[int] = []
    pack: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        u = max(remaining, key=lambda x: depth[x])
        d = parent[u] if parent[u] is not None else u
        dom.append(d)
        pack.append(u)
        remaining -= set(ball(g, d))
    return dom, pack


def random_forest(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> Graph:
    """A uniformly grown random forest on n vertices (each vertex attaches to
    an earlier vertex or starts a new component)."""
    edges: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for v in range(1, n):
        if rng.random() < 0.75:
            edges.append((rng.randrange(v), v))
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def check_collapse() -> None:
    print("5. gamma = rho for paths, interval graphs and forests")
    for n in range(1, 13):
        g = path_graph(n)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        assert gam == rho == (n + 2) // 3
    print("    paths P_1..P_12: gamma = rho = ceil(n/3) in every case")

    rng = random.Random(7)
    for _ in range(60):
        n = rng.randint(1, 8)
        iv = []
        for _ in range(n):
            a = rng.uniform(0, 10)
            iv.append((a, a + rng.uniform(0, 3)))
        g = interval_graph(iv)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        dom, pack = interval_greedy(iv)
        assert gam == rho
        assert is_dominating(g, dom) and is_packing(g, pack)
        assert len(dom) == len(pack) == gam
    print("    60 random interval graphs: gamma = rho, and the earliest-endpoint")
    print("    sweep returns a dominating set and a packing of that common size")

    for _ in range(60):
        g = random_forest(rng.randint(1, 9), rng)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        dom, pack = rooted_forest_greedy(g)
        assert gam == rho, (gam, rho)
        assert is_dominating(g, dom) and is_packing(g, pack)
        assert len(dom) == len(pack) == gam
    print("    60 random forests: the Meir-Moon equality gamma = rho holds, with")
    print("    the deepest-vertex sweep certifying both sides simultaneously")

    c4 = make_graph(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0)])
    print(f"    by contrast the 4-cycle (not a forest): gamma = "
          f"{domination_number(c4)}, rho = {packing_number(c4)}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Spread graphs: the ratio is unbounded over all finite graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def spread_graph(k: int, t: int) -> Graph:
    """Clique of k indices, all t-subsets as an independent set, i ~ S iff i in S.

    Indices are 0..k-1; the subset S is the vertex k + (its index in the list).
    """
    subsets = list(combinations(range(k), t))
    edges: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [(i, j) for i, j in combinations(range(k), 2)]
    for s_idx, s in enumerate(subsets):
        for i in s:
            edges.append((i, k + s_idx))
    return make_graph(k + len(subsets), edges)


def check_spread() -> None:
    print("6. Spread graphs: rho = 1 while gamma grows without bound")
    for m in (1, 2, 3):
        k, t = 2 * m, m + 1
        g = spread_graph(k, t)
        rho = packing_number(g)
        gam = domination_number(g)
        print(f"    m = {m} (k = {k} indices, t = {t}): "
              f"|V| = {len(g)}, rho = {rho}, gamma = {gam} >= {k - t + 1} = k-t+1")
        assert rho == 1
        assert gam >= k - t + 1
    print("    the ratio gamma/rho is therefore unbounded over all finite graphs")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The local packing bound of the plane
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def greedy_separated_points_in_disk(radius: float, sep: float,
                                    samples: int, rng: random.Random) -> int:
    """Greedily place points in a disk of the given radius, keeping them
    pairwise more than `sep` apart; returns how many were placed."""
    chosen: List[Tuple[float, float]] = []
    for _ in range(samples):
        theta = rng.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi)
        r = radius * math.sqrt(rng.random())
        p = (r * math.cos(theta), r * math.sin(theta))
        if all(math.dist(p, q) > sep for q in chosen):
            chosen.append(p)
    return len(chosen)


def hexagonal_separated_points_in_disk(radius: float, sep: float) -> int:
    """Count points of a triangular lattice of spacing slightly above `sep`
    that lie in the closed disk of the given radius, centred at a lattice point."""
    spacing = sep * 1.0000001
    count = 0
    reach = int(math.ceil(2 * radius / spacing)) + 2
    for i in range(-reach, reach + 1):
        for j in range(-reach, reach + 1):
            x = spacing * (i + j / 2.0)
            y = spacing * (math.sqrt(3) / 2.0) * j
            if math.hypot(x, y) <= radius + 1e-12:
                count += 1
    return count


def nineteen_point_configuration() -> List[Tuple[float, float]]:
    """An explicit set of 19 points in the closed disk of radius 2 that are
    pairwise more than 1 apart: the centre, a ring of 6 at radius 1.05, and a
    ring of 12 at radius 2 rotated by 15 degrees."""
    pts: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [(0.0, 0.0)]
    for j in range(6):
        a = 2 * math.pi * j / 6
        pts.append((1.05 * math.cos(a), 1.05 * math.sin(a)))
    for j in range(12):
        a = 2 * math.pi * (j + 0.5) / 12
        pts.append((2.0 * math.cos(a), 2.0 * math.sin(a)))
    return pts


def check_local_packing_bound() -> None:
    print("7. The local packing bound of the plane")
    print("    volume comparison: at most ((2*2+1)/1)^2 = 25 points, pairwise")
    print("    more than 1 apart, fit in a disk of radius 2; hence gamma <= 25*rho")
    rng = random.Random(11)
    best = max(greedy_separated_points_in_disk(2.0, 1.0, 4000, rng)
               for _ in range(40))
    hexa = hexagonal_separated_points_in_disk(2.0, 1.0)
    print(f"    best random greedy arrangement found: {best} points")
    print(f"    triangular-lattice arrangement:       {hexa} points")
    cfg = nineteen_point_configuration()
    min_sep = min(math.dist(p, q) for p, q in combinations(cfg, 2))
    max_rad = max(math.hypot(*p) for p in cfg)
    print(f"    explicit centre + 6 + 12 arrangement:  {len(cfg)} points, "
          f"minimum separation {min_sep:.4f} > 1, maximum radius {max_rad:.4f} <= 2")
    assert min_sep > 1.0 and max_rad <= 2.0 + 1e-12
    print("    (so the volume count 25 is lossy; the sharp value of this finite")
    print("     plane-packing constant is what would improve the theorem)")
    # the one-dimensional analogue is sharp at 4
    quad = [0.0, 1.1, 2.2, 3.3]
    sep_ok = all(abs(a - b) > 1 for a, b in combinations(quad, 2))
    near_ok = all(abs(x - 2.0) <= 2 for x in quad)
    print(f"    on the line the bound 4 is optimal: the points {quad} lie within")
    print(f"    distance 2 of 2 ({near_ok}) and are pairwise > 1 apart ({sep_ok})")
    assert sep_ok and near_ok
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Unit disk graphs: the bound gamma <= 25*rho in practice
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def check_unit_disk_instances() -> None:
    print("8. Random unit disk graphs: gamma <= 25*rho, with a large margin")
    rng = random.Random(4242)
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(120):
        n = rng.randint(4, 9)
        pts = [(rng.uniform(0, 2.5), rng.uniform(0, 2.5)) for _ in range(n)]
        g = unit_disk_graph(pts)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        assert gam <= 25 * rho
        worst = max(worst, gam / rho)
    print(f"    120 instances: the bound always holds; largest ratio seen "
          f"{worst:.3f}")
    print("    (the proven ceiling is 25, the best published constant is")
    print("     18*sqrt(3)/pi = %.3f, and the best known lower bound is 3)"
          % (18 * math.sqrt(3) / math.pi))
    print()


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("The domination-packing ratio: numerical demonstrations")
    print("=" * 72)
    print()
    check_duality_and_degree_bound()
    check_wagner()
    check_cycle4()
    check_collapse()
    check_spread()
    check_local_packing_bound()
    check_unit_disk_instances()
    print("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Exhaustive Verification of the Domination–Packing Landscape
demos.description: A single self-contained script that computes the domination number and the packing number exactly, by exhaustive search, and checks every structural claim of the theory on concrete instances: the universal inequality ρ ≤ γ and the degree bound γ ≤ (Δ+1)ρ on 200 random graphs; the Wagner graph (ρ = 1, γ = 3) and its disjoint copies (ρ = k, γ = 3k), together with the failure of any bound γ ≤ cρ + b with c < 3; the 4-cycle realized as a unit disk graph with γ = 2 and ρ = 1; the equality γ = ρ for paths, for 60 random interval graphs (with the earliest-endpoint sweep returning a dominating set and a packing of that common size) and for 60 random forests (with the deepest-vertex sweep); spread graphs with ρ = 1 and γ growing without bound; and the geometry behind the constant 25, including an explicit arrangement of 19 points in a disk of radius 2 that are pairwise more than 1 apart and the optimal 4-point arrangement on the line.
demos.code:
"""
Numerical demonstrations for the domination-packing ratio.

For a finite simple graph G on vertex set V, the radius-1 ball at v is
    B(v) = {v} union {u : u ~ v},
gamma(G) is the least size of a set meeting every B(v) via domination
(a transversal of the ball hypergraph), and rho(G) is the largest number
of pairwise disjoint balls (a matching of the same hypergraph).

This script verifies, by exhaustive computation on small instances:

  1. rho(G) <= gamma(G) for every graph (trivial duality).
  2. gamma <= (Delta + 1) * rho for every graph (degree bound).
  3. The Wagner graph V8 has rho = 1, gamma = 3, and k disjoint copies
     have rho = k, gamma = 3k, so the ratio 3 persists at every scale.
  4. The 4-cycle is a unit disk graph with gamma = 2, rho = 1.
  5. gamma = rho for paths, interval graphs and forests, with the
     earliest-endpoint and deepest-vertex greedy sweeps producing a
     dominating set and a packing of equal size.
  6. Spread graphs have rho = 1 and gamma >= k - t + 1, so the ratio is
     unbounded over all finite graphs.
  7. The local packing bound of the plane: how many points, pairwise more
     than 1 apart, fit in a disk of radius 2 (the volume count gives 25).

Everything is self-contained: only the Python standard library is used.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Vertex = int
Graph = Dict[Vertex, Set[Vertex]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic graph utilities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def make_graph(n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Build an undirected simple graph on {0, ..., n-1} from an edge list."""
    g: Graph = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        if u == v:
            raise ValueError("loops are not allowed")
        g[u].add(v)
        g[v].add(u)
    return g


def ball(g: Graph, v: Vertex) -> FrozenSet[Vertex]:
    """The radius-1 ball (closed neighbourhood) of v."""
    return frozenset({v} | g[v])


def is_dominating(g: Graph, d: Iterable[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """Does d meet the ball of every vertex?"""
    covered: Set[Vertex] = set()
    for x in d:
        covered |= ball(g, x)
    return covered == set(g)


def is_packing(g: Graph, p: Sequence[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """Are the balls of the vertices of p pairwise disjoint?"""
    for a, b in combinations(p, 2):
        if ball(g, a) & ball(g, b):
            return False
    return True


def domination_number(g: Graph) -> int:
    """gamma(G), by exhaustive search over subsets in increasing size."""
    vertices = list(g)
    for size in range(len(vertices) + 1):
        for cand in combinations(vertices, size):
            if is_dominating(g, cand):
                return size
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable: the whole vertex set dominates")


def packing_number(g: Graph) -> int:
    """rho(G), by exhaustive search over subsets in decreasing size."""
    vertices = list(g)
    for size in range(len(vertices), -1, -1):
        for cand in combinations(vertices, size):
            if is_packing(g, cand):
                return size
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable: the empty set is a packing")


def max_degree(g: Graph) -> int:
    return max((len(nbrs) for nbrs in g.values()), default=0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1-2. Trivial duality and the degree bound, on random graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def random_graph(n: int, p: float, rng: random.Random) -> Graph:
    edges = [(u, v) for u, v in combinations(range(n), 2) if rng.random() < p]
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def check_duality_and_degree_bound(trials: int = 200, n: int = 8) -> None:
    print("1-2. rho <= gamma and gamma <= (Delta+1)*rho on random graphs")
    rng = random.Random(20260820)
    worst_ratio = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        g = random_graph(n, rng.uniform(0.05, 0.6), rng)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        assert rho <= gam, (rho, gam)
        assert gam <= (max_degree(g) + 1) * rho, (gam, max_degree(g), rho)
        worst_ratio = max(worst_ratio, gam / rho)
    print(f"    {trials} random graphs on {n} vertices: both inequalities hold")
    print(f"    largest observed gamma/rho: {worst_ratio:.3f}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The Wagner graph V8 and its disjoint copies
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def wagner_graph() -> Graph:
    """V8 = Moebius ladder M4: the 8-cycle plus the four main diagonals."""
    edges = [(i, (i + 1) % 8) for i in range(8)] + [(i, i + 4) for i in range(4)]
    return make_graph(8, edges)


def disjoint_copies(g: Graph, k: int) -> Graph:
    """k disjoint copies of g, on vertices i*n + a for copy i and vertex a."""
    n = len(g)
    edges: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for i in range(k):
        for a in g:
            for b in g[a]:
                if a < b:
                    edges.append((i * n + a, i * n + b))
    return make_graph(k * n, edges)


def check_wagner() -> None:
    print("3. The Wagner graph V8 and the persistence of the ratio 3")
    w = wagner_graph()
    gam, rho = domination_number(w), packing_number(w)
    print(f"    V8: gamma = {gam}, rho = {rho}, ratio = {gam / rho:.0f}")
    assert (gam, rho) == (3, 1)
    meeting = all(ball(w, u) & ball(w, v) for u, v in combinations(range(8), 2))
    print(f"    every two closed neighbourhoods of V8 meet: {meeting}")
    for k in (1, 2, 3):
        wk = disjoint_copies(w, k)
        # gamma and rho are additive over components; verified directly for k <= 2
        rho_k = packing_number(wk) if k <= 3 else k
        gam_k = domination_number(wk) if k <= 2 else 3 * k
        print(f"    k = {k} copies: rho = {rho_k}, gamma = {gam_k}"
              f"{'' if k <= 2 else ' (gamma by additivity)'}")
        assert rho_k == k
        assert gam_k == 3 * k
    print("    no bound gamma <= c*rho + b can hold with c < 3:")
    for c, b in ((2, 5), (2, 50)):
        k = b + 1
        print(f"        c = {c}, b = {b}: at k = {k}, gamma = {3 * k} > "
              f"{c * k + b} = c*rho + b")
        assert 3 * k > c * k + b
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The 4-cycle as a unit disk graph
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def unit_disk_graph(points: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Graph:
    """Vertices are points; distinct points adjacent iff at distance <= 1."""
    n = len(points)
    edges = [
        (i, j)
        for i, j in combinations(range(n), 2)
        if math.dist(points[i], points[j]) <= 1.0
    ]
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def check_cycle4() -> None:
    print("4. The 4-cycle is a unit disk graph with gamma = 2, rho = 1")
    pts = [(0.0, 0.0), (0.8, 0.0), (0.8, 0.84), (0.0, 0.84)]
    g = unit_disk_graph(pts)
    sides = [math.dist(pts[i], pts[(i + 1) % 4]) for i in range(4)]
    diags = [math.dist(pts[0], pts[2]), math.dist(pts[1], pts[3])]
    print(f"    sides {['%.2f' % s for s in sides]} (all <= 1), "
          f"diagonals {['%.2f' % d for d in diags]} (both > 1)")
    gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
    print(f"    gamma = {gam}, rho = {rho}: the ratio already exceeds 1 in the plane")
    assert (gam, rho) == (2, 1)
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Interval graphs, paths and forests: gamma = rho by a greedy sweep
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def interval_graph(iv: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Graph:
    """Distinct vertices adjacent iff their closed intervals intersect."""
    n = len(iv)
    edges = [
        (i, j)
        for i, j in combinations(range(n), 2)
        if iv[i][0] <= iv[j][1] and iv[j][0] <= iv[i][1]
    ]
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def interval_greedy(iv: Sequence[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Earliest-endpoint sweep: returns (dominating set D, packing P), |D| = |P|.

    Repeatedly take the undominated vertex u whose interval ends first, put
    into D the vertex d whose interval ends last among those meeting u, bank
    u into P, and delete everything d dominates.
    """
    g = interval_graph(iv)
    remaining: Set[int] = set(range(len(iv)))
    dom: List[int] = []
    pack: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        u = min(remaining, key=lambda x: iv[x][1])
        meeting = [x for x in range(len(iv)) if iv[x][0] <= iv[u][1] <= iv[x][1]
                   or (iv[x][0] <= iv[u][1] and iv[u][0] <= iv[x][1])]
        d = max(meeting, key=lambda x: iv[x][1])
        dom.append(d)
        pack.append(u)
        remaining -= set(ball(g, d))
    return dom, pack


def path_graph(n: int) -> Graph:
    return make_graph(n, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(n - 1)])


def rooted_forest_greedy(g: Graph) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Deepest-vertex sweep on a forest: returns (dominating set, packing).

    Root each component, repeatedly take the deepest undominated vertex u,
    put its parent into D (or u itself if u is a root), bank u into P, and
    delete the ball of the chosen dominator.
    """
    parent: Dict[int, Optional[int]] = {}
    depth: Dict[int, int] = {}
    seen: Set[int] = set()
    for r in g:
        if r in seen:
            continue
        parent[r], depth[r] = None, 0
        seen.add(r)
        queue = [r]
        while queue:
            x = queue.pop(0)
            for y in g[x]:
                if y not in seen:
                    seen.add(y)
                    parent[y], depth[y] = x, depth[x] + 1
                    queue.append(y)
    remaining: Set[int] = set(g)
    dom: List[int] = []
    pack: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        u = max(remaining, key=lambda x: depth[x])
        d = parent[u] if parent[u] is not None else u
        dom.append(d)
        pack.append(u)
        remaining -= set(ball(g, d))
    return dom, pack


def random_forest(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> Graph:
    """A uniformly grown random forest on n vertices (each vertex attaches to
    an earlier vertex or starts a new component)."""
    edges: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    for v in range(1, n):
        if rng.random() < 0.75:
            edges.append((rng.randrange(v), v))
    return make_graph(n, edges)


def check_collapse() -> None:
    print("5. gamma = rho for paths, interval graphs and forests")
    for n in range(1, 13):
        g = path_graph(n)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        assert gam == rho == (n + 2) // 3
    print("    paths P_1..P_12: gamma = rho = ceil(n/3) in every case")

    rng = random.Random(7)
    for _ in range(60):
        n = rng.randint(1, 8)
        iv = []
        for _ in range(n):
            a = rng.uniform(0, 10)
            iv.append((a, a + rng.uniform(0, 3)))
        g = interval_graph(iv)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        dom, pack = interval_greedy(iv)
        assert gam == rho
        assert is_dominating(g, dom) and is_packing(g, pack)
        assert len(dom) == len(pack) == gam
    print("    60 random interval graphs: gamma = rho, and the earliest-endpoint")
    print("    sweep returns a dominating set and a packing of that common size")

    for _ in range(60):
        g = random_forest(rng.randint(1, 9), rng)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        dom, pack = rooted_forest_greedy(g)
        assert gam == rho, (gam, rho)
        assert is_dominating(g, dom) and is_packing(g, pack)
        assert len(dom) == len(pack) == gam
    print("    60 random forests: the Meir-Moon equality gamma = rho holds, with")
    print("    the deepest-vertex sweep certifying both sides simultaneously")

    c4 = make_graph(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0)])
    print(f"    by contrast the 4-cycle (not a forest): gamma = "
          f"{domination_number(c4)}, rho = {packing_number(c4)}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Spread graphs: the ratio is unbounded over all finite graphs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def spread_graph(k: int, t: int) -> Graph:
    """Clique of k indices, all t-subsets as an independent set, i ~ S iff i in S.

    Indices are 0..k-1; the subset S is the vertex k + (its index in the list).
    """
    subsets = list(combinations(range(k), t))
    edges: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [(i, j) for i, j in combinations(range(k), 2)]
    for s_idx, s in enumerate(subsets):
        for i in s:
            edges.append((i, k + s_idx))
    return make_graph(k + len(subsets), edges)


def check_spread() -> None:
    print("6. Spread graphs: rho = 1 while gamma grows without bound")
    for m in (1, 2, 3):
        k, t = 2 * m, m + 1
        g = spread_graph(k, t)
        rho = packing_number(g)
        gam = domination_number(g)
        print(f"    m = {m} (k = {k} indices, t = {t}): "
              f"|V| = {len(g)}, rho = {rho}, gamma = {gam} >= {k - t + 1} = k-t+1")
        assert rho == 1
        assert gam >= k - t + 1
    print("    the ratio gamma/rho is therefore unbounded over all finite graphs")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The local packing bound of the plane
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def greedy_separated_points_in_disk(radius: float, sep: float,
                                    samples: int, rng: random.Random) -> int:
    """Greedily place points in a disk of the given radius, keeping them
    pairwise more than `sep` apart; returns how many were placed."""
    chosen: List[Tuple[float, float]] = []
    for _ in range(samples):
        theta = rng.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi)
        r = radius * math.sqrt(rng.random())
        p = (r * math.cos(theta), r * math.sin(theta))
        if all(math.dist(p, q) > sep for q in chosen):
            chosen.append(p)
    return len(chosen)


def hexagonal_separated_points_in_disk(radius: float, sep: float) -> int:
    """Count points of a triangular lattice of spacing slightly above `sep`
    that lie in the closed disk of the given radius, centred at a lattice point."""
    spacing = sep * 1.0000001
    count = 0
    reach = int(math.ceil(2 * radius / spacing)) + 2
    for i in range(-reach, reach + 1):
        for j in range(-reach, reach + 1):
            x = spacing * (i + j / 2.0)
            y = spacing * (math.sqrt(3) / 2.0) * j
            if math.hypot(x, y) <= radius + 1e-12:
                count += 1
    return count


def nineteen_point_configuration() -> List[Tuple[float, float]]:
    """An explicit set of 19 points in the closed disk of radius 2 that are
    pairwise more than 1 apart: the centre, a ring of 6 at radius 1.05, and a
    ring of 12 at radius 2 rotated by 15 degrees."""
    pts: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [(0.0, 0.0)]
    for j in range(6):
        a = 2 * math.pi * j / 6
        pts.append((1.05 * math.cos(a), 1.05 * math.sin(a)))
    for j in range(12):
        a = 2 * math.pi * (j + 0.5) / 12
        pts.append((2.0 * math.cos(a), 2.0 * math.sin(a)))
    return pts


def check_local_packing_bound() -> None:
    print("7. The local packing bound of the plane")
    print("    volume comparison: at most ((2*2+1)/1)^2 = 25 points, pairwise")
    print("    more than 1 apart, fit in a disk of radius 2; hence gamma <= 25*rho")
    rng = random.Random(11)
    best = max(greedy_separated_points_in_disk(2.0, 1.0, 4000, rng)
               for _ in range(40))
    hexa = hexagonal_separated_points_in_disk(2.0, 1.0)
    print(f"    best random greedy arrangement found: {best} points")
    print(f"    triangular-lattice arrangement:       {hexa} points")
    cfg = nineteen_point_configuration()
    min_sep = min(math.dist(p, q) for p, q in combinations(cfg, 2))
    max_rad = max(math.hypot(*p) for p in cfg)
    print(f"    explicit centre + 6 + 12 arrangement:  {len(cfg)} points, "
          f"minimum separation {min_sep:.4f} > 1, maximum radius {max_rad:.4f} <= 2")
    assert min_sep > 1.0 and max_rad <= 2.0 + 1e-12
    print("    (so the volume count 25 is lossy; the sharp value of this finite")
    print("     plane-packing constant is what would improve the theorem)")
    # the one-dimensional analogue is sharp at 4
    quad = [0.0, 1.1, 2.2, 3.3]
    sep_ok = all(abs(a - b) > 1 for a, b in combinations(quad, 2))
    near_ok = all(abs(x - 2.0) <= 2 for x in quad)
    print(f"    on the line the bound 4 is optimal: the points {quad} lie within")
    print(f"    distance 2 of 2 ({near_ok}) and are pairwise > 1 apart ({sep_ok})")
    assert sep_ok and near_ok
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Unit disk graphs: the bound gamma <= 25*rho in practice
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def check_unit_disk_instances() -> None:
    print("8. Random unit disk graphs: gamma <= 25*rho, with a large margin")
    rng = random.Random(4242)
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(120):
        n = rng.randint(4, 9)
        pts = [(rng.uniform(0, 2.5), rng.uniform(0, 2.5)) for _ in range(n)]
        g = unit_disk_graph(pts)
        gam, rho = domination_number(g), packing_number(g)
        assert gam <= 25 * rho
        worst = max(worst, gam / rho)
    print(f"    120 instances: the bound always holds; largest ratio seen "
          f"{worst:.3f}")
    print("    (the proven ceiling is 25, the best published constant is")
    print("     18*sqrt(3)/pi = %.3f, and the best known lower bound is 3)"
          % (18 * math.sqrt(3) / math.pi))
    print()


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 72)
    print("The domination-packing ratio: numerical demonstrations")
    print("=" * 72)
    print()
    check_duality_and_degree_bound()
    check_wagner()
    check_cycle4()
    check_collapse()
    check_spread()
    check_local_packing_bound()
    check_unit_disk_instances()
    print("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Certified Approximation Quality of the Local-Cover Construction
demos.description: Measures how much slack the crude constant 25 leaves in practice. On random unit disk graphs the script computes the exact packing number, the exact domination number, and the size of the dominating set produced by the local-cover construction (a maximal packing, each of whose radius-2 neighbourhoods is dominated by a maximal independent subset), verifying the certified sandwich ρ ≤ γ ≤ |D| ≤ 25ρ on every instance and reporting the mean and worst observed values of γ/ρ and of the construction slack |D|/γ. The output shows that the guaranteed factor 25 is a far-from-tight worst-case ceiling, while the packing returned alongside the cover is a genuine per-instance lower-bound certificate.

algorithms.name: Local-Cover Domination with a Packing Certificate
algorithms.description: The algorithmic form of the local cover principle. It first builds a maximal packing greedily: scan the vertices, adding v whenever v is at graph distance at least 3 from every vertex already chosen. Maximality is exactly what is needed for the covering step: if some vertex were at distance at least 3 from all chosen centres it could be added, so the radius-2 neighbourhoods of the chosen centres cover the whole graph. For each centre p the algorithm then computes a maximal independent subset of the radius-2 neighbourhood of p; maximality makes that subset dominate the neighbourhood, and independence makes its vertices pairwise non-adjacent, hence — in a geometric representation — pairwise more than one unit apart inside a ball of radius 2. The union of these subsets is a dominating set. The output pair (D, P) satisfies |P| ≤ ρ(G) ≤ γ(G) ≤ |D|, and whenever the ambient metric space has local packing bound N (N = 25 in the plane, 5ⁿ in ℝⁿ, 4 on the line) also |D| ≤ N·|P|, i.e. an N-approximation with a per-instance certificate. Complexity: the packing costs one breadth-first search to depth 2 per vertex, O(|V|·(|V|+|E|)) in the worst case, and the independent sets cost O(Σ_p |T_p|²) where T_p is the radius-2 neighbourhood of the centre p.
algorithms.pseudocode:
Input:  finite graph G = (V, E)
Output: dominating set D and packing P with |P| <= gamma(G) <= |D|

1  P <- empty list;  Blocked <- empty set
2  for v in V (in any fixed order):
3      if v not in Blocked:
4          append v to P                       # v is at distance >= 3 from all chosen
5          Blocked <- Blocked union N2(v)      # N2(v) = ball of radius 2 around v
6  # P is a MAXIMAL packing, hence the sets N2(p), p in P, cover V
7  D <- empty set
8  for p in P:
9      I <- empty list
10     for u in N2(p) (in any fixed order):
11         if u is non-adjacent to every vertex of I:
12             append u to I                   # I stays independent
13     # I is a MAXIMAL independent subset of N2(p), hence dominates N2(p)
14     D <- D union I
15 return (D, P)

Guarantee: |P| <= rho(G) <= gamma(G) <= |D|, and |D| <= N * |P| whenever every
radius-2 ball of the ambient metric space holds at most N points pairwise > 1 apart.

algorithms.name: Earliest-Endpoint Sweep for Interval Graphs
algorithms.description: An exact min–max algorithm for interval graphs, where each vertex v carries a closed interval [l(v), r(v)] and two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when their intervals meet. The sweep repeatedly takes the still-undominated vertex u whose interval ends first, selects as dominator the vertex d whose interval ends last among those meeting u, banks u as a packing centre, and deletes everything d dominates. The invariant is that every surviving vertex starts strictly to the right of r(d), and since r(d) is maximal among the vertices meeting u, no survivor's interval can meet any interval of the ball of u; hence the banked centres are pairwise at graph distance at least 3 and form a packing. Because exactly one dominator is spent per banked centre, the output satisfies |D| = |P|, and combining with the universal inequality ρ ≤ γ gives |P| ≤ ρ ≤ γ ≤ |D| = |P|. The algorithm therefore returns simultaneously an optimal dominating set and an optimal packing, each certifying the optimality of the other, and constitutes a constructive proof that γ = ρ for every interval graph. Complexity: O(n log n) after sorting by right endpoint, or O(n²) with the direct implementation.
algorithms.pseudocode:
Input:  intervals [l(v), r(v)] for v in V (adjacency: intervals meet)
Output: dominating set D and packing P with |D| = |P| = gamma = rho

1  Remaining <- V;  D <- empty list;  P <- empty list
2  while Remaining is nonempty:
3      u <- argmin over Remaining of r(.)          # interval ending first
4      B(u) <- { x in V : l(x) <= r(u) and l(u) <= r(x) }
5      d <- argmax over B(u) of r(.)               # reaches farthest to the right
6      append d to D;  append u to P
7      Remaining <- Remaining \ B(d)
8  return (D, P)

Invariant: every vertex left in Remaining starts strictly right of r(d) >= r(x)
for all x in B(u); hence B(u) is disjoint from the ball of every later centre.
algorithms.code:
"""Earliest-endpoint sweep for interval graphs: an exact min-max algorithm.

For a graph given by closed intervals [l(v), r(v)] (adjacency = intervals
meet), the sweep returns a dominating set D and a packing P with |D| = |P|.
Since a packing never exceeds the domination number, both are optimal:
    |P| <= rho(G) <= gamma(G) <= |D| = |P|,
so the algorithm proves gamma(G) = rho(G) constructively, in O(n log n).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Interval = Tuple[float, float]


def meets(a: Interval, b: Interval) -> bool:
    """Do the closed intervals a and b intersect?"""
    return a[0] <= b[1] and b[0] <= a[1]


def closed_ball(iv: Sequence[Interval], u: int) -> Set[int]:
    """The radius-1 ball of u: all vertices whose interval meets u's."""
    return {x for x in range(len(iv)) if meets(iv[x], iv[u])}


def interval_sweep(iv: Sequence[Interval]) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Return (D, P) with D dominating, P a packing, and |D| = |P|.

    Greedy step: among the still-undominated vertices take u with the smallest
    right endpoint; among all vertices meeting u take d with the largest right
    endpoint; output d into D, bank u into P, delete everything d dominates.
    Every survivor starts strictly to the right of r(d), which is exactly what
    makes the banked centres pairwise more than 2 apart in graph distance.
    """
    remaining: Set[int] = set(range(len(iv)))
    dom: List[int] = []
    pack: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        u = min(remaining, key=lambda x: iv[x][1])
        d = max(closed_ball(iv, u), key=lambda x: iv[x][1])
        dom.append(d)
        pack.append(u)
        remaining -= closed_ball(iv, d)
    return dom, pack


def verify(iv: Sequence[Interval], dom: Sequence[int], pack: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    covered: Set[int] = set()
    for d in dom:
        covered |= closed_ball(iv, d)
    if covered != set(range(len(iv))):
        return False
    for i, a in enumerate(pack):
        for b in pack[i + 1:]:
            if closed_ball(iv, a) & closed_ball(iv, b):
                return False
    return len(dom) == len(pack)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    intervals: List[Interval] = [
        (0.0, 1.0), (0.5, 2.0), (1.8, 2.4), (2.3, 5.0),
        (4.5, 4.8), (4.7, 6.0), (6.5, 7.0), (6.8, 9.0),
    ]
    D, P = interval_sweep(intervals)
    print(f"intervals: {intervals}")
    print(f"dominating set D = {D}")
    print(f"packing        P = {P}")
    print(f"|D| = |P| = {len(D)}, hence gamma = rho = {len(D)}")
    assert verify(intervals, D, P)

algorithms.name: Deepest-Vertex Sweep on Forests (Constructive Meir–Moon)
algorithms.description: The acyclic instance of the same greedy schema, and a linear-time constructive proof of the Meir–Moon theorem γ(F) = ρ(F). Root every component by breadth-first search, then repeatedly take the deepest still-undominated vertex u, put its parent d into the dominating set (or u itself when u is a root), bank u as a packing centre, and delete the closed neighbourhood of d. Correctness rests on two properties of acyclic graphs: adjacent vertices have different depths, and every vertex has at most one parent — in each case a second geodesic would close a cycle. Consequently a neighbour of u among the remaining vertices can only be its parent (children are deeper, contradicting maximality), and a remaining vertex at distance exactly 2 from u either hangs off the parent of u or would be a second parent of a child of u, hence equals u; everything relevant therefore lies inside the closed neighbourhood of d. One dominator is spent per banked centre, so |D| = |P| and both are optimal. Complexity: O(|V| + |E|) after the initial breadth-first search.
algorithms.pseudocode:
Input:  forest F = (V, E)
Output: dominating set D and packing P with |D| = |P| = gamma(F) = rho(F)

1  (parent, depth) <- BFS from one root per connected component
2  Remaining <- V;  D <- empty list;  P <- empty list
3  while Remaining is nonempty:
4      u <- argmax over Remaining of depth(.)      # a deepest undominated vertex
5      d <- parent(u) if parent(u) exists else u
6      append d to D;  append u to P
7      Remaining <- Remaining \ B(d)               # B(d) = closed neighbourhood
8  return (D, P)

Invariant: every remaining vertex within distance 2 of u lies in B(d), because in an
acyclic graph adjacent vertices have distinct depths and each vertex has one parent.
algorithms.code:
"""Deepest-vertex sweep on forests: a constructive proof of gamma = rho.

Root every component of a forest.  Repeatedly take the deepest undominated
vertex u, put its parent d into the dominating set (or u itself when u is a
root), bank u into the packing, and delete the ball of d.  The two structural
facts about acyclic graphs -- adjacent vertices have different depths, and
every vertex has at most one parent -- guarantee that the closed neighbourhood
of d contains every vertex of the current set at distance at most 2 from u.
Hence the banked centres form a packing and |D| = |P|, giving the Meir-Moon
theorem gamma(F) = rho(F) in linear time after a breadth-first search.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import deque
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Vertex = int
Graph = Dict[Vertex, Set[Vertex]]


def ball(g: Graph, v: Vertex) -> FrozenSet[Vertex]:
    return frozenset({v} | g[v])


def root_forest(g: Graph) -> Tuple[Dict[Vertex, Optional[Vertex]], Dict[Vertex, int]]:
    """Breadth-first search from one root per component; returns parents/depths."""
    parent: Dict[Vertex, Optional[Vertex]] = {}
    depth: Dict[Vertex, int] = {}
    seen: Set[Vertex] = set()
    for r in sorted(g):
        if r in seen:
            continue
        parent[r], depth[r] = None, 0
        seen.add(r)
        queue = deque([r])
        while queue:
            x = queue.popleft()
            for y in sorted(g[x]):
                if y not in seen:
                    seen.add(y)
                    parent[y], depth[y] = x, depth[x] + 1
                    queue.append(y)
    return parent, depth


def forest_sweep(g: Graph) -> Tuple[List[Vertex], List[Vertex]]:
    """Return (D, P): a dominating set and a packing with |D| = |P|."""
    parent, depth = root_forest(g)
    remaining: Set[Vertex] = set(g)
    dom: List[Vertex] = []
    pack: List[Vertex] = []
    while remaining:
        u = max(remaining, key=lambda x: (depth[x], x))
        p = parent[u]
        d = u if p is None else p
        dom.append(d)
        pack.append(u)
        remaining -= set(ball(g, d))
    return dom, pack


def is_acyclic(g: Graph) -> bool:
    """A graph is a forest iff every component has one fewer edge than vertices."""
    seen: Set[Vertex] = set()
    for r in g:
        if r in seen:
            continue
        comp: Set[Vertex] = set()
        queue = deque([r])
        seen.add(r)
        while queue:
            x = queue.popleft()
            comp.add(x)
            for y in g[x]:
                if y not in seen:
                    seen.add(y)
                    queue.append(y)
        edges = sum(len(g[x] & comp) for x in comp) // 2
        if edges != len(comp) - 1:
            return False
    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # a caterpillar tree on 11 vertices
    edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4),
             (0, 5), (1, 6), (2, 7), (3, 8), (4, 9), (4, 10)]
    g: Graph = {v: set() for v in range(11)}
    for a, b in edges:
        g[a].add(b)
        g[b].add(a)
    assert is_acyclic(g)
    D, P = forest_sweep(g)
    print(f"dominating set D = {D}")
    print(f"packing        P = {P}")
    print(f"|D| = |P| = {len(D)}, so gamma = rho = {len(D)} (Meir-Moon)")
    covered: Set[int] = set()
    for d in D:
        covered |= ball(g, d)
    assert covered == set(g)
    assert all(not (ball(g, a) & ball(g, b)) for a, b in combinations(P, 2))

visualizations.name: The Local Cover in Action on a Unit Disk Graph
visualizations.description: Draws a random unit disk graph and overlays the three ingredients of the local cover principle: the pairwise disjoint radius-1 balls of a maximal packing (blue), the radius-2 neighbourhoods of the same centres (orange) which necessarily cover every vertex, and the dominating set harvested as a maximal independent subset of each neighbourhood (green rings). The caption reports the certified sandwich |P| ≤ γ ≤ |D| obtained from the single run.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: a unit disk graph with a maximal packing and the local cover.

Draws a random unit disk graph, highlights a maximal packing (whose radius-1
balls are pairwise disjoint), shades the radius-2 neighbourhood of each packing
centre -- these cover the whole graph, which is why gamma <= N*rho -- and marks
the dominating set produced by the local-cover construction.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from collections import deque
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Dict, List, Set, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Graph = Dict[int, Set[int]]


def unit_disk_graph(pts: List[Tuple[float, float]]) -> Graph:
    g: Graph = {i: set() for i in range(len(pts))}
    for i, j in combinations(range(len(pts)), 2):
        if math.dist(pts[i], pts[j]) <= 1.0:
            g[i].add(j)
            g[j].add(i)
    return g


def within_two(g: Graph, p: int) -> Set[int]:
    seen = {p}
    q = deque([(p, 0)])
    while q:
        x, d = q.popleft()
        if d == 2:
            continue
        for y in g[x]:
            if y not in seen:
                seen.add(y)
                q.append((y, d + 1))
    return seen


def maximal_packing(g: Graph) -> List[int]:
    chosen: List[int] = []
    blocked: Set[int] = set()
    for v in sorted(g):
        if v not in blocked:
            chosen.append(v)
            blocked |= within_two(g, v)
    return chosen


def maximal_independent_subset(g: Graph, t: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    chosen: List[int] = []
    for v in t:
        if all(v not in g[u] for u in chosen):
            chosen.append(v)
    return chosen


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(2026)
    pts = [(rng.uniform(0, 4), rng.uniform(0, 3)) for _ in range(45)]
    g = unit_disk_graph(pts)
    packing = maximal_packing(g)
    dom: Set[int] = set()
    for p in packing:
        dom |= set(maximal_independent_subset(g, sorted(within_two(g, p))))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
    for i, j in combinations(range(len(pts)), 2):
        if j in g[i]:
            ax.plot([pts[i][0], pts[j][0]], [pts[i][1], pts[j][1]],
                    color="0.82", lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    for p in packing:
        ax.add_patch(plt.Circle(pts[p], 2.0, color="tab:orange",
                                alpha=0.05, zorder=0))
        ax.add_patch(plt.Circle(pts[p], 1.0, color="tab:blue",
                                alpha=0.10, zorder=0))
    xs, ys = zip(*pts)
    ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=28, color="0.35", zorder=3, label="vertices")
    ax.scatter([pts[d][0] for d in dom], [pts[d][1] for d in dom],
               s=110, facecolors="none", edgecolors="tab:green", lw=2.0,
               zorder=4, label=f"dominating set (|D| = {len(dom)})")
    ax.scatter([pts[p][0] for p in packing], [pts[p][1] for p in packing],
               s=90, color="tab:red", marker="*", zorder=5,
               label=f"packing centres (|P| = {len(packing)})")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_title("Unit disk graph: disjoint radius-1 balls (blue) and the\n"
                 "radius-2 neighbourhoods (orange) that cover everything")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", framealpha=0.95)
    ax.set_xlabel(f"certified bounds:  {len(packing)} = |P| <= gamma <= |D| = {len(dom)}")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("unit_disk_local_cover.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote unit_disk_local_cover.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Landscape of the Ratio and the Geometry Behind the Constant
visualizations.description: A two-panel figure. The left panel plots the domination number against the packing number for the extremal families — disjoint Wagner copies (γ = 3ρ at every scale), paths, forests and interval graphs (γ = ρ), and spread graphs (ρ = 1 with γ unbounded) — together with the proven unit disk ceiling γ ≤ 25ρ. The right panel shows the geometric input to that ceiling: an explicit configuration of 19 points inside a disk of radius 2 that are pairwise more than 1 apart, with the disjoint half-unit disks that the area count compares, illustrating why the constant 25 is lossy.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the landscape of the domination-packing ratio.

Left panel: the exact values of gamma and rho on the extremal families --
disjoint copies of the Wagner graph (gamma = 3*rho at every scale), paths
(gamma = rho), and spread graphs (rho = 1 with gamma growing) -- plotted
against the packing number.

Right panel: the geometric input.  The centre + ring-of-6 + ring-of-12
configuration of 19 points inside a disk of radius 2, pairwise more than 1
apart, which is what makes the volume bound 25 lossy.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from itertools import combinations
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def nineteen_points() -> List[Tuple[float, float]]:
    pts: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [(0.0, 0.0)]
    for j in range(6):
        a = 2 * math.pi * j / 6
        pts.append((1.05 * math.cos(a), 1.05 * math.sin(a)))
    for j in range(12):
        a = 2 * math.pi * (j + 0.5) / 12
        pts.append((2.0 * math.cos(a), 2.0 * math.sin(a)))
    return pts


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.6))

    ks = list(range(1, 13))
    ax1.plot(ks, [3 * k for k in ks], "o-", color="tab:red",
             label="Wagner unions:  gamma = 3*rho")
    ax1.plot(ks, ks, "s-", color="tab:green",
             label="paths / forests / interval graphs:  gamma = rho")
    ax1.plot([1] * len(ks), ks, "^", color="tab:purple",
             label="spread graphs:  rho = 1, gamma unbounded")
    ax1.plot(ks, [25 * k for k in ks], "--", color="tab:blue",
             label="unit disk ceiling:  gamma <= 25*rho")
    ax1.set_xlabel("packing number  rho")
    ax1.set_ylabel("domination number  gamma")
    ax1.set_title("How far apart can covering and packing be?")
    ax1.set_yscale("log")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left")

    pts = nineteen_points()
    sep = min(math.dist(p, q) for p, q in combinations(pts, 2))
    ax2.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), 2.0, color="tab:orange", alpha=0.10))
    for p in pts:
        ax2.add_patch(plt.Circle(p, 0.5, color="tab:blue", alpha=0.18))
    ax2.scatter(*zip(*pts), s=25, color="black", zorder=3)
    ax2.set_xlim(-2.7, 2.7)
    ax2.set_ylim(-2.7, 2.7)
    ax2.set_aspect("equal")
    ax2.set_title(f"{len(pts)} points in a disk of radius 2,\n"
                  f"pairwise {sep:.3f} > 1 apart "
                  "(the volume count only gives 25)")
    ax2.axis("off")

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("domination_packing_landscape.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote domination_packing_landscape.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The earliest-endpoint sweep

Each vertex of an interval graph is a closed interval; two vertices are adjacent when their intervals meet. The greedy sweep repeatedly takes the still-undominated vertex whose interval ends first (banking it as a packing centre), pays for it with the vertex whose interval ends last among those meeting it (a dominator), and deletes everything that dominator covers. Because the two lists always have the same length, and a packing can never be larger than a dominating set is small, this single sweep proves γ = ρ for every interval graph — and the same idea, with "deepest vertex / its parent" in place of "earliest endpoint / farthest-reaching neighbour", proves it for every forest.

interactive_layout:
# Covering vs. Packing: a guided tour of the domination–packing ratio Two dual questions live on every network. **Cover it.** Choose as *few* nodes as possible so that every node is chosen or sits next to a chosen one. The minimum number is the **domination number** $\gamma(G)$. **Spread out on it.** Choose as *many* nodes as possible so that their one-hop zones never overlap. The maximum number is the **packing number** $\rho(G)$. They are two sides of one hypergraph: writing $B(v) = \{v\} \cup \{u : u \sim v\}$ for the radius-$1$ ball at $v$, a dominating set is a *transversal* of the family $\{B(v)\}$ and a packing is a *matching* of it. One inequality is free — and the whole subject is about how badly the other one can fail. > **Free direction.** $\rho(G) \le \gamma(G)$ for every finite graph. > > Every packing centre needs a dominator inside its own ball, and different centres have disjoint balls, so the dominators are distinct. --- ## 1. Play with it first Before any theory: place transmitters, watch $\gamma$ and $\rho$ move. Everything in the panel is computed exactly. {{interactive_demo:0}} Things worth trying: * Put all points **on a line**. No matter how you arrange them, $\gamma = \rho$. That is not luck — it is a theorem, and Section 4 proves it. * Load the **4-cycle** preset: a square with short sides and long diagonals. Here $\gamma = 2$ while $\rho = 1$: the four closed neighbourhoods pairwise intersect, so only one packing zone fits, yet no single vertex reaches the opposite corner. This is the smallest planar witness that the ratio leaves $1$. * Cluster many points inside a small blob. The graph becomes a clique: $\gamma = \rho = 1$. Density is not what breaks the duality — *spread* is.
Why do balls meet exactly at distance ≤ 2? (the fact behind every proof below) If $w \in B(u) \cap B(v)$, then $w$ is $u$ or a neighbour of $u$, and likewise for $v$, so $u$ and $v$ are joined by a walk of length at most $2$. Conversely a walk of length $\le 2$ from $u$ to $v$ produces a common element (take $u$, $v$, or the midpoint). Hence $$B(u)\cap B(v) \neq \emptyset \iff \operatorname{dist}(u,v)\le 2,$$ so a **packing is exactly a set of vertices pairwise at distance $\ge 3$**, and the region that matters around a vertex is its **radius-$2$ neighbourhood**.
--- ## 2. Without geometry, all bets are off It is tempting to think $\gamma$ and $\rho$ can never drift far apart. They can — arbitrarily far. Fix $k < 2t$ and build the **spread graph**: $k$ indices forming a clique, all $t$-element subsets of the indices forming an independent set, and $i \sim S$ exactly when $i \in S$. * Since $k < 2t$, any two $t$-subsets intersect. Consequently *every* two balls meet, so $\rho = 1$. * But a $t$-subset avoiding all the indices you selected can only be dominated by putting *itself* into the dominating set, and there are many such subsets: $\gamma \ge k - t + 1$. With $k = 2m$ and $t = m + 1$: $\rho = 1$ and $\gamma \ge m$, for every $m$. So no inequality $\gamma \le c\rho + b$ can hold across all finite graphs, and a **graph class** is not a convenience — it is a necessity. --- ## 3. The engine: cover locally, count globally Here is the single lemma from which every upper bound in this tour follows. > **Local Cover Principle.** If for every vertex $p$ there is a set $D_p$ of at most $c$ vertices dominating everything at distance $\le 2$ from $p$, then $\gamma(G) \le c\,\rho(G)$.
Proof (three lines, and the only trick is "maximum ⇒ maximal") Let $P$ be a packing of maximum size $\rho(G)$. If some vertex $v$ were at distance $\ge 3$ from every $p \in P$, then $P \cup \{v\}$ would be a strictly larger packing. So the radius-$2$ neighbourhoods of $P$ cover $V$. Replace each by its dominator set and take the union: $$D := \bigcup_{p\in P} D_p, \qquad |D| \le \sum_{p \in P}|D_p| \le c\,|P| = c\,\rho(G),$$ and $D$ dominates everything. $\blacksquare$
Two immediate consequences: * Taking $D_p = B(p)$ gives $\gamma \le (\Delta+1)\rho$ for **every** graph of maximum degree $\Delta$. * In a geometric graph, take instead a **maximal independent subset** of the radius-$2$ neighbourhood: maximality makes it dominate, independence makes the corresponding points pairwise more than $1$ apart, and all of them live in a disk of radius $2$. That last observation compresses the entire graph problem into one finite geometry question, which we can now run as an algorithm. {{algorithm:0}} Here is what the algorithm is really doing, drawn on an actual instance: the blue disks are the pairwise disjoint one-hop zones of the packing, the pale orange disks are the radius-$2$ neighbourhoods that must cover everything, and the green circles are the dominators harvested from each of them. {{visualization:0}}
From geometry to a constant: the volume count How many points, pairwise more than $1$ apart, fit in a disk of radius $2$? Put a disk of radius $\tfrac12$ around each: they are disjoint and all contained in a disk of radius $\tfrac52$. Comparing areas, $$\#\text{points} \le \frac{(5/2)^2}{(1/2)^2} = 25 .$$ Hence **$\gamma \le 25\,\rho$ for every unit disk graph**, and the identical argument in $\mathbb{R}^n$ gives $\gamma \le 5^n\rho$. Say that a metric space has *local packing bound* $N$ when no radius-$2$ ball holds more than $N$ points pairwise more than $1$ apart; then any graph drawn in such a space satisfies $\gamma \le N\rho$. Geometry enters through exactly one number.
Read the guarantee operationally: in a wireless network, *either* there are $k$ mutually non-interfering nodes, *or* $25k$ relays already cover everything. And the algorithm hands you both objects — the cover and the certificate. {{demo:1}} --- ## 4. On a line, greed is perfect The volume count on the real line gives $4$, and $4$ is genuinely the best that method can do: the points $0, 1.1, 2.2, 3.3$ all sit within distance $2$ of the point $2$ and are pairwise more than $1$ apart. Yet the truth on the line is not $4$ but $1$ — and it holds for all **interval graphs**, where each vertex is an arbitrary closed interval and adjacency means "the intervals meet". > **Interval Graph Theorem.** $\gamma(G) = \rho(G)$ for every finite interval graph. Step through the sweep that proves it. Each move banks one packing centre and spends exactly one dominator — so the two sets end with the same size, and each certifies the optimality of the other. {{interactive_demo:1}} {{algorithm:1}}
Why the banked centres really are a packing Let $u$ be the undominated vertex whose interval ends first and $d$ the vertex ending last among those meeting $u$. Every vertex surviving the deletion of $B(d)$ starts strictly to the right of $r(d)$. Since $r(d) \ge r(x)$ for every $x \in B(u)$, no survivor's interval can meet any interval of $B(u)$ — that is precisely $B(u) \cap B(q) = \emptyset$ for every later centre $q$. Hence the banked centres are pairwise at distance $\ge 3$. $\blacksquare$
A concrete instance: the path $P_n$, with vertex $i$ at the real number $i$, has $$\gamma(P_n) = \rho(P_n) = \left\lceil \frac{n}{3}\right\rceil,$$ the packing being every third vertex, whose balls $\{i-1,i,i+1\}$ are disjoint. --- ## 5. One criterion, two classical theorems Strip the sweep down to what it actually used. Say $G$ has a **greedy dominator** if, for every nonempty set $S$ of vertices, some $u \in S$ has the property that everything in $S$ within distance $2$ of $u$ fits inside a *single* closed neighbourhood $B(d)$. > **Collapse Theorem.** A greedy dominator forces $\gamma(G) = \rho(G)$. Interval graphs have one (earliest endpoint / farthest-reaching neighbour). Forests have one too — and that is a classical theorem in disguise. > **Meir–Moon Theorem.** $\gamma(F) = \rho(F)$ for every finite forest $F$. {{algorithm:2}}
The forest rule, and the two facts about trees that make it work Root each component and take for $u$ a *deepest* vertex of $S$, for $d$ its parent. Two properties of acyclic graphs finish the argument: 1. **Adjacent vertices have different depths** — two geodesics from the root plus the connecting edge would otherwise close a cycle. 2. **Every vertex has at most one parent** — two parents would likewise close a cycle. So a neighbour of $u$ inside $S$ can only be its parent (children are deeper, contradicting maximality), and a vertex of $S$ at distance exactly $2$ from $u$ either hangs off $u$'s parent or would be a second parent of a child of $u$, hence equals $u$. Everything lands in $B(d)$. $\blacksquare$
The criterion is not vacuous: the $4$-cycle fails it, since $\gamma(C_4) = 2 \neq 1 = \rho(C_4)$ — and, amusingly, that failure re-proves that $C_4$ is not a forest. --- ## 6. How large must the constant be? Upper bounds are only half the story. Meet the **Wagner graph** $V_8$ (the Möbius ladder $M_4$): the $8$-cycle $0-1-\cdots-7-0$ plus the four long diagonals $i \sim i+4$. * All eight closed neighbourhoods pairwise intersect, so $\rho(V_8) = 1$. * Two vertices never suffice to dominate, while $\{0,1,2\}$ does: $\gamma(V_8) = 3$. One small graph proves little, so take $k$ disjoint copies. Balls never leave their copy, so both invariants are additive: $$\rho = k, \qquad \gamma = 3k .$$ The ratio $3$ therefore survives at *every* scale, and no bound $\gamma \le c\rho + b$ can hold with $c < 3$ — the additive slack $b$ is powerless against a family whose ratio is scale-invariant. (For unit disk graphs the $4$-cycle already forces the constant to be at least $2$.) {{demo:0}} --- ## 7. The whole landscape at a glance {{visualization:1}} | class | ratio $\gamma/\rho$ | | --- | --- | | all finite graphs | unbounded | | maximum degree $\Delta$ | $\le \Delta+1$ | | forests, trees | $= 1$ | | interval and unit interval graphs, paths | $= 1$ | | unit interval graphs, by the metric method alone | $\le 4$ (optimal for that method) | | unit disk graphs | $\ge 2$, and $\le 25$ by the area count | | unit ball graphs in $\mathbb{R}^n$ | $\le 5^n$ | | classes containing large Wagner unions | $\ge 3$ | The area count is the only lossy step in the whole chain: an explicit configuration — the centre, a ring of six points at radius $1.05$, and a ring of twelve at radius $2$ offset by $15°$ — already fits $19$ pairwise-separated points into a disk of radius $2$, and $19$ is believed to be exactly the maximum. Improving the theorem is *exactly* this finite plane-packing problem. Sharper arguments in the literature reach $\gamma \le 5\rho$ for planar graphs and $\gamma \le (18\sqrt3/\pi)\rho \approx 9.924\rho$ for unit disk graphs, against a best known lower bound of $3$; the optimal constants remain open. Further reading on the surrounding notions: [domination in graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominating_set), [unit disk graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_disk_graph), [interval graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_graph), the [Erdős–Pósa property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93P%C3%B3sa_theorem), and the [Wagner graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagner_graph). --- ## 8. The one-sentence summary Domination and packing are dual; without structure their gap is unbounded; bounded degree caps it at $\Delta+1$; one-dimensional or acyclic structure closes it completely; and a Euclidean embedding caps it by a single geometric constant — the number of $1$-separated points that fit in a ball of twice the adjacency radius. What decides which world you are in is whether one vertex can ever pay for the whole radius-$2$ neighbourhood of the next packing centre.
